# API Endpoint Documentation

## User Endpoints

GET /api/v1/users
This endpoint returns a paginated list of all users in the system.
Authentication is required via Bearer token.
Query parameters: limit (default 20), offset (default 0), sort_by (name, created_at)
Returns: Array of user objects with id, name, email, created_at fields.

POST /api/v1/users
Creates a new user account in the system.
Requires admin role authentication.
Request body must include: name (string), email (string), role (string).
Optional fields: phone, department, manager_id.
Returns: Created user object with generated id.

GET /api/v1/users/{id}
Retrieves a single user by their unique identifier.
Authentication required. Users can only view their own profile unless admin.
Path parameter: id (UUID format required).
Returns: Full user object including preferences and metadata.

DELETE /api/v1/users/{id}
Permanently removes a user from the system.
Requires admin role. Cannot delete yourself.
Returns: 204 No Content on success.
Caution: This action cannot be undone.

input.content:
## Redis Caching Implementation Notes

Cache invalidation strategy uses TTL-based expiry with write-through
on mutations. Key schema: `{entity_type}:{user_id}:{entity_id}`.

Connection pooling configured via redis-py with max_connections=50.
Sentinel support enabled for HA deployments. Failover timeout: 30s.

Serialization: msgpack for binary efficiency. Compression disabled
due to latency overhead (tested: ~2ms penalty per op).

Monitoring: Redis INFO stats exported to Prometheus via redis_exporter.
Key metrics: connected_clients, used_memory, keyspace_hits/misses.

Known issues:
- Race condition possible during cache warm-up (mitigated by locks)
- Large values (>1MB) cause fragmentation; consider chunking
- Pub/sub not suitable for reliable messaging; use Kafka instead

arguments.title: Beginner’s Guide to Redis Caching
arguments.description: A friendly introduction to what Redis caching is, why it helps, and how this project uses it.
arguments.content:
## A Beginner’s Guide to Redis Caching

### What is a cache?

A cache is a place to keep useful information temporarily so it can be found quickly. Imagine keeping frequently used books on your desk instead of walking to the library every time you need one.

Redis is a fast data store that can act as this kind of short-term storage. An application can check Redis first for information. If the information is there, it can use it right away. If not, it can get the information from its usual source and save a copy in Redis for next time.

### Why use Redis?

Caching can make an application respond faster and reduce repeated work. It can also reduce the number of requests sent to a database or another slower service. Cached information is temporary, though, so the application needs a plan for keeping it current.

### How this project uses Redis

- **Information expires automatically:** Each cached item has a time limit (TTL). When the time is up, Redis removes it, so old copies do not stay forever.
- **Updates refresh the cache:** When the application changes information, it also updates the cached copy. This helps people see recent changes.
- **Keys identify cached items:** Each item gets a name based on its type and the relevant user and item IDs. This makes it easier to find the right copy.
- **Connections are reused:** The application keeps a pool of up to 50 Redis connections ready to use. Reusing connections avoids repeatedly setting them up.
- **Redis can switch to a backup:** Sentinel helps the system notice when a Redis server is unavailable and move to another one. The configured failover timeout is 30 seconds.
- **Data is stored compactly:** The application uses MessagePack, a format for turning data into a compact form Redis can store and retrieve. Compression is off because testing found it added about 2 milliseconds to each operation.

### Keeping an eye on Redis

Monitoring tools collect information about Redis and send it to Prometheus, where the team can track it. Useful measures include how many clients are connected, how much memory Redis is using, and how often requests find or miss cached data.

### Things to watch out for

- **Starting the cache can cause a rush of requests:** If many requests try to fill the cache at once, they may overlap. Locks help make sure only one fills a given item at a time.
- **Very large items can waste memory:** Values larger than 1 MB may make memory use less efficient. Splitting them into smaller pieces may help.
- **Redis messages are not guaranteed delivery:** Redis publish-and-subscribe can be useful for quick notifications, but it should not be relied on when every message must arrive. This project uses Kafka for that kind of dependable messaging.

In short, Redis is a fast temporary shelf for information the application often needs. It helps the application work faster, while expiry and update rules help keep the shelf from becoming stale.

A cache is a place to keep useful information temporarily so it can be found quickly. Imagine keeping frequently used books on your desk instead of walking to the library every time you need one.

Redis is a fast data store that can act as this kind of short-term storage. An application can check Redis first for information. If the information is there, it can use it right away. If not, it can get the information from its usual source and save a copy in Redis for next time.

### Why use Redis?

Caching can make an application respond faster and reduce repeated work. It can also reduce the number of requests sent to a database or another slower service. Cached information is temporary, though, so the application needs a plan for keeping it current.

### How this project uses Redis

- **Information expires automatically:** Each cached item has a time limit (TTL). When the time is up, Redis removes it, so old copies do not stay forever.
- **Updates refresh the cache:** When the application changes information, it also updates the cached copy. This helps people see recent changes.
- **Keys identify cached items:** Each item gets a name based on its type and the relevant user and item IDs. This makes it easier to find the right copy.
- **Connections are reused:** The application keeps a pool of up to 50 Redis connections ready to use. Reusing connections avoids repeatedly setting them up.
- **Redis can switch to a backup:** Sentinel helps the system notice when a Redis server is unavailable and move to another one. The configured failover timeout is 30 seconds.
- **Data is stored compactly:** The application uses MessagePack, a format for turning data into a compact form Redis can store and retrieve. Compression is off because testing found it added about 2 milliseconds to each operation.

### Keeping an eye on Redis

Monitoring tools collect information about Redis and send it to Prometheus, where the team can track it. Useful measures include how many clients are connected, how much memory Redis is using, and how often requests find or miss cached data.

### Things to watch out for

- **Starting the cache can cause a rush of requests:** If many requests try to fill the cache at once, they may overlap. Locks help make sure only one fills a given item at a time.
- **Very large items can waste memory:** Values larger than 1 MB may make memory use less efficient. Splitting them into smaller pieces may help.
- **Redis messages are not guaranteed delivery:** Redis publish-and-subscribe can be useful for quick notifications, but it should not be relied on when every message must arrive. This project uses Kafka for that kind of dependable messaging.

In short, Redis is a fast temporary shelf for information the application often needs. It helps the application work faster, while expiry and update rules help keep the shelf from becoming stale.

input.content:
# API Endpoint Documentation

## User Endpoints

GET /api/v1/users
This endpoint returns a paginated list of all users in the system.
Authentication is required via Bearer token.
Query parameters: limit (default 20), offset (default 0), sort_by (name, created_at)
Returns: Array of user objects with id, name, email, created_at fields.

POST /api/v1/users
Creates a new user account in the system.
Requires admin role authentication.
Request body must include: name (string), email (string), role (string).
Optional fields: phone, department, manager_id.
Returns: Created user object with generated id.

GET /api/v1/users/{id}
Retrieves a single user by their unique identifier.
Authentication required. Users can only view their own profile unless admin.
Path parameter: id (UUID format required).
Returns: Full user object including preferences and metadata.

DELETE /api/v1/users/{id}
Permanently removes a user from the system.
Requires admin role. Cannot delete yourself.
Returns: 204 No Content on success.
Caution: This action cannot be undone.

## Redis Caching Implementation Notes

Cache invalidation strategy uses TTL-based expiry with write-through
on mutations. Key schema: `{entity_type}:{user_id}:{entity_id}`.

Connection pooling configured via redis-py with max_connections=50.
Sentinel support enabled for HA deployments. Failover timeout: 30s.

Serialization: msgpack for binary efficiency. Compression disabled
due to latency overhead (tested: ~2ms penalty per op).

Monitoring: Redis INFO stats exported to Prometheus via redis_exporter.
Key metrics: connected_clients, used_memory, keyspace_hits/misses.

Known issues:
- Race condition possible during cache warm-up (mitigated by locks)
- Large values (>1MB) cause fragmentation; consider chunking
- Pub/sub not suitable for reliable messaging; use Kafka instead

arguments.title: Beginner’s Guide to Redis Caching
arguments.description: A friendly introduction to what Redis caching is, why it helps, and how this project uses it.
arguments.content:
# A Beginner’s Guide to Redis Caching

## What is caching?

Imagine you often need the same information. Instead of going back to a large filing cabinet every time, you keep a copy nearby so you can find it quickly. A cache works in a similar way: it keeps temporary copies of information that an application is likely to need again.

Redis is a fast service that can hold these copies in memory. Because memory is quick to access, an application can often get cached information faster than fetching it from its main data store. This can make pages and features feel more responsive and reduce repeated work for the main system.

## How this project uses Redis

- **Copies expire automatically:** Each cached item has a time limit (a TTL). When the time is up, Redis removes it, so old copies do not stay around forever.
- **Updates refresh the cache:** When the application changes information, it also updates the cached copy. This helps people see recent changes rather than an outdated version.
- **Keys help find items:** Each copy gets a name based on its kind of information and the relevant user and item IDs. This gives the application a consistent way to look it up.
- **Connections are reused:** The application keeps a pool of ready-to-use connections instead of repeatedly opening new ones. The pool allows up to 50 connections, helping manage requests efficiently.
- **Redis can have a backup plan:** For high-availability setups, Sentinel helps the application find a working Redis server if the current one fails. The configured failover timeout is 30 seconds.
- **Data is stored compactly:** The project uses MessagePack, a compact format for turning data into something Redis can store and return. It does not compress the data, because testing showed compression added about 2 milliseconds to each operation.

## Keeping an eye on performance

Redis reports information about its health and activity. The project sends these measurements to Prometheus, a monitoring system, using a tool called `redis_exporter`. Useful measurements include how many clients are connected, how much memory Redis is using, and how often requests find or miss a cached item.

A **cache hit** means the requested copy was found. A **cache miss** means it was not, so the application needs to fetch the information elsewhere and may save a copy for next time.

## Things to watch out for

- **Several requests may try to fill the same empty cache at once.** This can cause extra work during warm-up. Locks help ensure that only one request fills a particular cache entry at a time.
- **Very large cached items can use memory inefficiently.** Values larger than 1 MB may contribute to memory fragmentation. Splitting them into smaller pieces may help.
- **Redis messages are not guaranteed to be delivered reliably.** Its publish-and-subscribe feature is useful for simple live updates, but important messages should use a system designed to keep and reliably deliver them, such as Kafka.

## The main idea

Redis caching is a way to keep frequently needed information close at hand. It can make an application faster and reduce repeated requests to its main data store. Caches are temporary copies, though, so the application needs clear rules for refreshing and expiring them—and should monitor memory and performance as it grows.

# API Endpoint Documentation

## User Endpoints

GET /api/v1/users
This endpoint returns a paginated list of all users in the system.
Authentication is required via Bearer token.
Query parameters: limit (default 20), offset (default 0), sort_by (name, created_at)
Returns: Array of user objects with id, name, email, created_at fields.

POST /api/v1/users
Creates a new user account in the system.
Requires admin role authentication.
Request body must include: name (string), email (string), role (string).
Optional fields: phone, department, manager_id.
Returns: Created user object with generated id.

GET /api/v1/users/{id}
Retrieves a single user by their unique identifier.
Authentication required. Users can only view their own profile unless admin.
Path parameter: id (UUID format required).
Returns: Full user object including preferences and metadata.

DELETE /api/v1/users/{id}
Permanently removes a user from the system.
Requires admin role. Cannot delete yourself.
Returns: 204 No Content on success.
Caution: This action cannot be undone.

input.content:
## Redis Caching Implementation Notes

Cache invalidation strategy uses TTL-based expiry with write-through
on mutations. Key schema: `{entity_type}:{user_id}:{entity_id}`.

Connection pooling configured via redis-py with max_connections=50.
Sentinel support enabled for HA deployments. Failover timeout: 30s.

Serialization: msgpack for binary efficiency. Compression disabled
due to latency overhead (tested: ~2ms penalty per op).

Monitoring: Redis INFO stats exported to Prometheus via redis_exporter.
Key metrics: connected_clients, used_memory, keyspace_hits/misses.

Known issues:
- Race condition possible during cache warm-up (mitigated by locks)
- Large values (>1MB) cause fragmentation; consider chunking
- Pub/sub not suitable for reliable messaging; use Kafka instead

arguments.title: Beginner’s Guide to Redis Caching
arguments.description: A friendly introduction to what Redis caching does, why it is useful, and how this project uses it.
arguments.content:
# A Beginner’s Guide to Redis Caching

## What is caching?

Imagine a busy kitchen where the cook keeps popular ingredients close at hand instead of walking to the pantry every time. A cache works in a similar way: it keeps copies of useful information somewhere quick to reach, so an app can respond faster without repeatedly doing slower work.

Redis is a tool often used as this fast storage space. It keeps information ready for a short time, such as details an app has recently needed.

## Why use Redis caching?

Without a cache, an app may need to fetch or calculate the same information again and again. Keeping a temporary copy can make common requests quicker and reduce repeated work for other systems, such as a database. Caches are temporary helpers, though—not the permanent source of truth—so the app needs a plan for keeping cached copies up to date.

## How this project uses Redis

- **Copies expire automatically:** Each cached item has a time limit (TTL). When that time is up, Redis removes it so the app can fetch fresh information when needed.
- **Changes update the cache:** When the app changes information, it also updates the cached copy. This helps prevent people from seeing an old version.
- **Keys are labeled consistently:** A key is the name used to find an item in the cache. This project names keys using the kind of item, the user, and the item’s ID—for example, `profile:42:7`.
- **Connections are reused:** The app keeps a managed set of connections to Redis, with a limit of 50. Reusing connections avoids setting up a new one for every request.
- **Redis can switch servers:** For high-availability setups, Sentinel helps the app find a working Redis server if the current one fails. The configured failover timeout is 30 seconds.
- **Data is stored compactly:** Cached data is encoded in a compact format called MessagePack. Compression is turned off because testing showed it adds about 2 milliseconds to each operation.
- **The system is monitored:** Redis activity is sent to Prometheus, a monitoring tool. The team watches how many clients are connected, how much memory Redis uses, and how often requests find or miss cached data.

## Things to watch out for

- When the cache is being filled for the first time, multiple requests may try to do the same work. Locks help ensure only one request fills an item at a time.
- Very large cached items (over 1 MB) can use memory inefficiently. Splitting them into smaller pieces may help.
- Redis pub/sub sends messages to listeners, but it does not guarantee that every message will be received. For messages that must be reliably delivered, this project uses Kafka instead.

In short, Redis caching is like keeping frequently needed information within easy reach. It can make an app faster and reduce repeated work, as long as cached copies are refreshed and monitored carefully.

# A Beginner’s Guide to Redis Caching

## What is caching?

Imagine a busy kitchen where the cook keeps popular ingredients close at hand instead of walking to the pantry every time. A cache works in a similar way: it keeps copies of useful information somewhere quick to reach, so an app can respond faster without repeatedly doing slower work.

Redis is a tool often used as this fast storage space. It keeps information ready for a short time, such as details an app has recently needed.

## Why use Redis caching?

Without a cache, an app may need to fetch or calculate the same information again and again. Keeping a temporary copy can make common requests quicker and reduce repeated work for other systems, such as a database. Caches are temporary helpers, though—not the permanent source of truth—so the app needs a plan for keeping cached copies up to date.

## How this project uses Redis

- **Copies expire automatically:** Each cached item has a time limit (TTL). When that time is up, Redis removes it so the app can fetch fresh information when needed.
- **Changes update the cache:** When the app changes information, it also updates the cached copy. This helps prevent people from seeing an old version.
- **Keys are labeled consistently:** A key is the name used to find an item in the cache. This project names keys using the kind of item, the user, and the item’s ID—for example, `profile:42:7`.
- **Connections are reused:** The app keeps a managed set of connections to Redis, with a limit of 50. Reusing connections avoids setting up a new one for every request.
- **Redis can switch servers:** For high-availability setups, Sentinel helps the app find a working Redis server if the current one fails. The configured failover timeout is 30 seconds.
- **Data is stored compactly:** Cached data is encoded in a compact format called MessagePack. Compression is turned off because testing showed it adds about 2 milliseconds to each operation.
- **The system is monitored:** Redis activity is sent to Prometheus, a monitoring tool. The team watches how many clients are connected, how much memory Redis uses, and how often requests find or miss cached data.

## Things to watch out for

- When the cache is being filled for the first time, multiple requests may try to do the same work. Locks help ensure only one request fills an item at a time.
- Very large cached items (over 1 MB) can use memory inefficiently. Splitting them into smaller pieces may help.
- Redis pub/sub sends messages to listeners, but it does not guarantee that every message will be received. For messages that must be reliably delivered, this project uses Kafka instead.

In short, Redis caching is like keeping frequently needed information within easy reach. It can make an app faster and reduce repeated work, as long as cached copies are refreshed and monitored carefully.

# API Endpoint Documentation

## User Endpoints

GET /api/v1/users
This endpoint returns a paginated list of all users in the system.
Authentication is required via Bearer token.
Query parameters: limit (default 20), offset (default 0), sort_by (name, created_at)
Returns: Array of user objects with id, name, email, created_at fields.

POST /api/v1/users
Creates a new user account in the system.
Requires admin role authentication.
Request body must include: name (string), email (string), role (string).
Optional fields: phone, department, manager_id.
Returns: Created user object with generated id.

GET /api/v1/users/{id}
Retrieves a single user by their unique identifier.
Authentication required. Users can only view their own profile unless admin.
Path parameter: id (UUID format required).
Returns: Full user object including preferences and metadata.

DELETE /api/v1/users/{id}
Permanently removes a user from the system.
Requires admin role. Cannot delete yourself.
Returns: 204 No Content on success.
Caution: This action cannot be undone.

## Redis Caching Implementation Notes

Cache invalidation strategy uses TTL-based expiry with write-through
on mutations. Key schema: `{entity_type}:{user_id}:{entity_id}`.

Connection pooling configured via redis-py with max_connections=50.
Sentinel support enabled for HA deployments. Failover timeout: 30s.

Serialization: msgpack for binary efficiency. Compression disabled
due to latency overhead (tested: ~2ms penalty per op).

Monitoring: Redis INFO stats exported to Prometheus via redis_exporter.
Key metrics: connected_clients, used_memory, keyspace_hits/misses.

Known issues:
- Race condition possible during cache warm-up (mitigated by locks)
- Large values (>1MB) cause fragmentation; consider chunking

Cache invalidation strategy uses TTL-based expiry with write-through
on mutations. Key schema: `{entity_type}:{user_id}:{entity_id}`.

Connection pooling configured via redis-py with max_connections=50.
Sentinel support enabled for HA deployments. Failover timeout: 30s.

Serialization: msgpack for binary efficiency. Compression disabled
due to latency overhead (tested: ~2ms penalty per op).

Monitoring: Redis INFO stats exported to Prometheus via redis_exporter.
Key metrics: connected_clients, used_memory, keyspace_hits/misses.

Known issues:
- Race condition possible during cache warm-up (mitigated by locks)
- Large values (>1MB) cause fragmentation; consider chunking
- Pub/sub not suitable for reliable messaging; use Kafka instead

arguments.description: A simple introduction to Redis caching, how this setup works, and the trade-offs to keep in mind.
arguments.content:
## Redis Caching: A Beginner-Friendly Guide

### What is a cache?

A cache is a fast, temporary place to keep copies of information that an app may need again soon. Instead of fetching the same information from a slower database every time, the app can often get it from the cache. This can make the app feel quicker and reduce repeated work.

Redis is a tool commonly used to store this temporary information. It keeps data ready for quick access, but the cache is not meant to be the only permanent home for important information.

### How this setup works

- **Cached information expires:** Each cached entry has a time limit (TTL). When the time is up, Redis removes it so the app can fetch a fresh copy when needed.
- **Changes update the cache:** When the app changes information, it also updates the cache. This helps people see recent changes rather than an old saved copy.
- **Keys help find entries:** Each cached item gets a label built from its type and related user and item IDs, such as `profile:42:7`. This gives the app a consistent way to look it up.
- **Connections are reused:** The app keeps a pool of Redis connections ready instead of opening a new connection for every request. The pool can hold up to 50 connections.
- **Service continues through some failures:** For high-availability deployments, Redis Sentinel watches the Redis service and helps switch to a healthy server if one fails. The configured failover timeout is 30 seconds.
- **Data is stored compactly:** The app uses MessagePack, a compact format for turning data into something Redis can store and return. Compression is turned off because testing found it added about 2 milliseconds to each operation.

### Keeping an eye on Redis

Redis statistics are sent to Prometheus using `redis_exporter`, so the team can monitor how the cache is doing. Useful measurements include how many clients are connected, how much memory Redis uses, and how often requests find an item in the cache versus miss and need to fetch it elsewhere.

### Things to watch out for

- **A busy start-up can cause duplicate work:** When many requests try to fill an empty cache at once, they may all fetch the same data. Locks help make one request do the work while others wait.
- **Very large entries can be awkward:** Values larger than 1 MB may use memory inefficiently. Splitting them into smaller pieces may help.
- **Redis messaging is not guaranteed delivery:** Redis publish-and-subscribe is useful for quick notifications, but it should not be relied on when every message must arrive. Use Kafka for that kind of reliable message delivery.

In short, Redis caching helps an app serve frequently needed information quickly. Expiration and updates help keep cached copies fresh, while monitoring and a few safeguards help the system stay healthy.

# API Endpoint Documentation

## User Endpoints

GET /api/v1/users
This endpoint returns a paginated list of all users in the system.
Authentication is required via Bearer token.
Query parameters: limit (default 20), offset (default 0), sort_by (name, created_at)
Returns: Array of user objects with id, name, email, created_at fields.

POST /api/v1/users
Creates a new user account in the system.
Requires admin role authentication.
Request body must include: name (string), email (string), role (string).
Optional fields: phone, department, manager_id.
Returns: Created user object with generated id.

GET /api/v1/users/{id}
Retrieves a single user by their unique identifier.
Authentication required. Users can only view their own profile unless admin.
Path parameter: id (UUID format required).
Returns: Full user object including preferences and metadata.

DELETE /api/v1/users/{id}
Permanently removes a user from the system.
Requires admin role. Cannot delete yourself.
Returns: 204 No Content on success.
Caution: This action cannot be undone.

## Redis Caching Implementation Notes

Cache invalidation strategy uses TTL-based expiry with write-through
on mutations. Key schema: `{entity_type}:{user_id}:{entity_id}`.

Connection pooling configured via redis-py with max_connections=50.
Sentinel support enabled for HA deployments. Failover timeout: 30s.

Serialization: msgpack for binary efficiency. Compression disabled
due to latency overhead (tested: ~2ms penalty per op).

Monitoring: Redis INFO stats exported to Prometheus via redis_exporter.
Key metrics: connected_clients, used_memory, keyspace_hits/misses.

Known issues:
- Race condition possible during cache warm-up (mitigated by locks)
- Large values (>1MB) cause fragmentation; consider chunking
- Pub/sub not suitable for reliable messaging; use Kafka instead

arguments.description: A friendly introduction to what Redis caching is, why we use it, and how this setup works.
arguments.content:
# A Beginner’s Guide to Redis Caching

## What is caching?

Imagine you often need the same information, such as a user’s profile. Instead of looking it up from the main database every time, an application can keep a temporary copy somewhere it can reach quickly. That temporary copy is called a **cache**.

**Redis** is a tool that stores information in memory, which makes it useful for keeping these quick-to-retrieve copies. A cache can help an application respond faster and reduce repeated work for the main database.

## How this cache works

- **Each saved item gets a time limit.** We set an expiry time (TTL), so old copies are eventually removed rather than kept forever.
- **Changes update the cache.** When the application changes something, it also updates the cached copy. This helps people see recent information.
- **Keys help us find items.** Each cached item has a name built from its kind, the user, and the item’s ID—for example, `profile:42:7`. This keeps entries organized and distinct.
- **Redis connections are reused.** The app keeps a pool of up to 50 connections available, rather than repeatedly opening new ones. This can make requests more efficient.

## Keeping the service available

For deployments that need extra reliability, Redis can be set up with Sentinel. Sentinel watches the Redis servers and helps the application switch to a working server if the current one fails. The configured failover timeout is 30 seconds.

## Storing data efficiently

Cached data is encoded with MessagePack, a compact format for turning data into bytes and back again. We leave compression off because testing found it added about 2 milliseconds to each operation—more delay than this setup wants to introduce.

## Watching performance

Redis reports information about its health and activity. We send these measurements to Prometheus using `redis_exporter`. Useful measurements include how many clients are connected, how much memory Redis is using, and how often requests find or miss a cached item.

A **cache hit** means the requested item was found in Redis. A **cache miss** means it was not there, so the application needs to get it another way, usually from the main database.

## Things to keep in mind

- When the cache is first filled, two requests might try to load the same item at once. Locks help prevent that race.
- Very large items (over 1 MB) can make Redis memory less tidy. Splitting them into smaller pieces may help.
- Redis pub/sub is useful for quick notifications, but it does not guarantee that every message will be delivered. For messages that must be reliably kept and processed, use Kafka instead.

In short, Redis caching keeps frequently needed information close at hand so an application can work faster, while expiry rules, updates, monitoring, and reliability measures help keep the cache useful and manageable.

- Very large items (over 1 MB) can make Redis memory less tidy. Splitting them into smaller pieces may help.
- Redis pub/sub is useful for quick notifications, but it does not guarantee that every message will be delivered. For messages that must be reliably kept and processed, use Kafka instead.

In short, Redis caching keeps frequently needed information close at hand so an application can work faster, while expiry rules, updates, monitoring, and reliability measures help keep the cache useful and manageable.

input.content:
# API Endpoint Documentation

## User Endpoints

GET /api/v1/users
This endpoint returns a paginated list of all users in the system.
Authentication is required via Bearer token.
Query parameters: limit (default 20), offset (default 0), sort_by (name, created_at)
Returns: Array of user objects with id, name, email, created_at fields.

POST /api/v1/users
Creates a new user account in the system.
Requires admin role authentication.
Request body must include: name (string), email (string), role (string).
Optional fields: phone, department, manager_id.
Returns: Created user object with generated id.

GET /api/v1/users/{id}
Retrieves a single user by their unique identifier.
Authentication required. Users can only view their own profile unless admin.
Path parameter: id (UUID format required).
Returns: Full user object including preferences and metadata.

DELETE /api/v1/users/{id}
Permanently removes a user from the system.
Requires admin role. Cannot delete yourself.
Returns: 204 No Content on success.
Caution: This action cannot be undone.

## Redis Caching Implementation Notes

Cache invalidation strategy uses TTL-based expiry with write-through
on mutations. Key schema: `{entity_type}:{user_id}:{entity_id}`.

Connection pooling configured via redis-py with max_connections=50.
Sentinel support enabled for HA deployments. Failover timeout: 30s.

Serialization: msgpack for binary efficiency. Compression disabled
due to latency overhead (tested: ~2ms penalty per op).

Monitoring: Redis INFO stats exported to Prometheus via redis_exporter.
Key metrics: connected_clients, used_memory, keyspace_hits/misses.

Known issues:
- Race condition possible during cache warm-up (mitigated by locks)
- Large values (>1MB) cause fragmentation; consider chunking
- Pub/sub not suitable for reliable messaging; use Kafka instead

arguments.description: A friendly introduction to what Redis caching is, why it helps, and how this setup works.
arguments.content:
# A Beginner’s Guide to Redis Caching

## What is caching?

A cache is a place to keep a temporary copy of information so it can be found quickly. Redis is a fast service that stores this information in memory. Instead of repeatedly asking a slower database for the same data, an application can first check Redis and reuse a saved copy when it is available.

This can make an application respond faster and reduce the amount of work its database has to do.

## How this setup works

- **Saved information expires:** Each cached item is kept for a limited time. This helps prevent old copies from sticking around forever.
- **Changes update the cache:** When the application changes something, it also updates the saved copy. This helps keep the cache in step with the main data.
- **Keys identify saved items:** Each item gets a name based on its kind, the user, and the item’s ID. This makes it easier to find the right copy.
- **Connections are reused:** The application keeps a pool of up to 50 Redis connections ready to use. Reusing connections avoids repeatedly setting them up.
- **A backup plan is available:** Redis Sentinel helps the system switch to another Redis server if the current one has a problem. The configured failover timeout is 30 seconds.
- **Data is stored compactly:** The setup uses MessagePack, a format for turning data into a compact form. Compression is off because testing showed it added about 2 milliseconds to each operation.

## Keeping an eye on Redis

Redis reports information about its health and activity. A monitoring tool sends these measurements to Prometheus so the team can track them. Useful measurements include how many clients are connected, how much memory Redis is using, and how often requests find or miss cached data.

## Things to watch out for

- **Starting with an empty cache:** Many requests arriving at once while the cache is being filled can cause a rush of work. Locks help make sure only a limited number of tasks fill the same data at a time.
- **Very large items:** Values larger than 1 MB can use memory inefficiently. Splitting them into smaller pieces may help.
- **Messages that must not be lost:** Redis pub/sub is a way to send messages to listeners, but it does not guarantee that every message will be delivered. For important, reliable messaging, this setup uses Kafka instead.

In short, Redis caching keeps frequently needed data close at hand. Used carefully, it can make an application faster while reducing repeated work for the main database.

# API Endpoint Documentation

## User Endpoints

GET /api/v1/users
This endpoint returns a paginated list of all users in the system.
Authentication is required via Bearer token.
Query parameters: limit (default 20), offset (default 0), sort_by (name, created_at)
Returns: Array of user objects with id, name, email, created_at fields.

POST /api/v1/users
Creates a new user account in the system.
Requires admin role authentication.
Request body must include: name (string), email (string), role (string).
Optional fields: phone, department, manager_id.
Returns: Created user object with generated id.

GET /api/v1/users/{id}
Retrieves a single user by their unique identifier.
Authentication required. Users can only view their own profile unless admin.
Path parameter: id (UUID format required).
Returns: Full user object including preferences and metadata.

DELETE /api/v1/users/{id}
Permanently removes a user from the system.
Requires admin role. Cannot delete yourself.
Returns: 204 No Content on success.
Caution: This action cannot be undone.

## Redis Caching Implementation Notes

Cache invalidation strategy uses TTL-based expiry with write-through
on mutations. Key schema: `{entity_type}:{user_id}:{entity_id}`.

Connection pooling configured via redis-py with max_connections=50.
Sentinel support enabled for HA deployments. Failover timeout: 30s.

Serialization: msgpack for binary efficiency. Compression disabled
due to latency overhead (tested: ~2ms penalty per op).

Monitoring: Redis INFO stats exported to Prometheus via redis_exporter.
Key metrics: connected_clients, used_memory, keyspace_hits/misses.

Known issues:
- Race condition possible during cache warm-up (mitigated by locks)
- Large values (>1MB) cause fragmentation; consider chunking
- Pub/sub not suitable for reliable messaging; use Kafka instead

arguments.description: A friendly introduction to what Redis caching does, why it helps, and how this project uses it.
arguments.content:
# A Beginner’s Guide to Redis Caching

## What is a cache?

A cache is a place to keep useful information temporarily so it can be found quickly next time. Think of it like keeping frequently used items on your desk instead of walking to a storage room every time you need them.

Redis is a tool that stores this information in fast-access memory. An application can check Redis before doing slower work, such as looking up information in a database. If the information is there, the application can use it right away. If not, it can fetch the information, use it, and save a copy in Redis for next time.

## Why use Redis caching?

Caching can make an application respond faster and reduce repeated work for databases and other services. It is especially useful when the same information is requested often. Cached information is temporary, though, so the application needs a plan for keeping it fresh.

## How this project uses Redis

- **Cached information expires:** Each cached entry has a time limit (TTL). When the time is up, Redis removes it, so the application can fetch a fresh copy when needed.
- **Changes update the cache:** When the application changes information, it also updates the cached copy. This helps prevent people from seeing old information after an update.
- **Keys are labeled consistently:** Each entry’s name follows this pattern: `{entity_type}:{user_id}:{entity_id}`. The parts identify what kind of thing is stored and which user and item it belongs to.
- **Connections are reused:** The application keeps a pool of up to 50 Redis connections ready to use. Reusing connections avoids repeatedly setting up a new connection for each request.
- **High availability is supported:** Redis Sentinel helps the application find a working Redis server if the main one has a problem. The configured failover timeout is 30 seconds.
- **Data is stored compactly:** Cached data is encoded with MessagePack, a format that stores data in a compact binary form. Compression is turned off because testing showed it added about 2 milliseconds to each operation.
- **Health is monitored:** Redis statistics are sent to Prometheus through `redis_exporter`. The team watches how many clients are connected, how much memory Redis uses, and how often requests find or miss cached entries.

## Things to watch out for

- **Starting the cache can cause a rush:** When the cache is being filled for the first time, several requests might try to fetch the same information at once. Locks help make sure only one request does the work at a time.
- **Very large entries can be troublesome:** Values larger than 1 MB may use memory inefficiently. Splitting them into smaller pieces may help.
- **Redis messages are not guaranteed delivery:** Redis pub/sub is useful for quick notifications, but messages can be missed. Use Kafka when messages must be delivered reliably.

## In short

Redis caching keeps frequently needed information close at hand, helping an application work faster and avoid repeating the same lookups. Because cached data can expire or become outdated, the application also needs clear rules for updating it, monitoring it, and handling problems.

Caching can make an application respond faster and reduce repeated work for databases and other services. It is especially useful when the same information is requested often. Cached information is temporary, though, so the application needs a plan for keeping it fresh.

## How this project uses Redis

- **Cached information expires:** Each cached entry has a time limit (TTL). When the time is up, Redis removes it, so the application can fetch a fresh copy when needed.
- **Changes update the cache:** When the application changes information, it also updates the cached copy. This helps prevent people from seeing old information after an update.
- **Keys are labeled consistently:** Each entry’s name follows this pattern: `{entity_type}:{user_id}:{entity_id}`. The parts identify what kind of thing is stored and which user and item it belongs to.
- **Connections are reused:** The application keeps a pool of up to 50 Redis connections ready to use. Reusing connections avoids repeatedly setting up a new connection for each request.

- **Data is stored compactly:** Cached data is encoded with MessagePack, a format that stores data in a compact binary form. Compression is turned off because testing showed it added about 2 milliseconds to each operation.
- **Health is monitored:** Redis statistics are sent to Prometheus through `redis_exporter`. The team watches how many clients are connected, how much memory Redis uses, and how often requests find or miss cached entries.

## Things to watch out for

- **Starting the cache can cause a rush:** When the cache is being filled for the first time, several requests might try to fetch the same information at once. Locks help make sure only one request does the work at a time.

- **Redis messages are not guaranteed delivery:** Redis pub/sub is useful for quick notifications, but messages can be missed. Use Kafka when messages must be delivered reliably.

## In short

Redis caching keeps frequently needed information close at hand, helping an application work faster and avoid repeating the same lookups. Because cached data can expire or become outdated, the application also needs clear rules for updating it, monitoring it, and handling problems.

# API Endpoint Documentation

## User Endpoints

GET /api/v1/users
This endpoint returns a paginated list of all users in the system.
Authentication is required via Bearer token.
Query parameters: limit (default 20), offset (default 0), sort_by (name, created_at)
Returns: Array of user objects with id, name, email, created_at fields.

POST /api/v1/users
Creates a new user account in the system.
Requires admin role authentication.
Request body must include: name (string), email (string), role (string).
Optional fields: phone, department, manager_id.
Returns: Created user object with generated id.

GET /api/v1/users/{id}
Retrieves a single user by their unique identifier.
Authentication required. Users can only view their own profile unless admin.
Path parameter: id (UUID format required).
Returns: Full user object including preferences and metadata.

DELETE /api/v1/users/{id}
Permanently removes a user from the system.
Requires admin role. Cannot delete yourself.
Returns: 204 No Content on success.
Caution: This action cannot be undone.

## Redis Caching Implementation Notes

Cache invalidation strategy uses TTL-based expiry with write-through
on mutations. Key schema: `{entity_type}:{user_id}:{entity_id}`.

Connection pooling configured via redis-py with max_connections=50.
Sentinel support enabled for HA deployments. Failover timeout: 30s.

Serialization: msgpack for binary efficiency. Compression disabled
due to latency overhead (tested: ~2ms penalty per op).

Monitoring: Redis INFO stats exported to Prometheus via redis_exporter.
Key metrics: connected_clients, used_memory, keyspace_hits/misses.

Known issues:
- Race condition possible during cache warm-up (mitigated by locks)
- Large values (>1MB) cause fragmentation; consider chunking
- Pub/sub not suitable for reliable messaging; use Kafka instead

arguments.title: A Beginner’s Guide to Redis Caching
arguments.description: A friendly introduction to how Redis caching works, why it helps, and how this project uses it.
arguments.content:
# A Beginner’s Guide to Redis Caching

## What is a cache?

A cache is a fast, temporary place to keep information that an app may need again soon. Instead of repeatedly fetching the same information from a slower database or another service, the app can look in the cache first. This can make responses quicker and reduce work for the systems behind the app.

Redis is a tool often used to provide this kind of fast storage. Think of it like a handy shelf: the app puts commonly needed information there so it is easy to grab. The cache is helpful, but it should not be treated as the only permanent copy of important data.

## How this project uses Redis

- **Give cached information an expiry time.** Each saved item is set to expire after a period of time. This helps prevent old information from staying in the cache forever.
- **Refresh the cache when data changes.** When the app updates something, it also updates the cached copy. This helps users see current information.
- **Use clear names for saved items.** Keys follow the pattern `{entity_type}:{user_id}:{entity_id}`. In plain terms, the name includes what kind of thing it is and which user and item it belongs to. This makes entries easier to identify and keeps them organized.

## Keeping Redis available

The app reuses a managed set of connections to Redis rather than opening a brand-new connection for every request. The pool can hold up to 50 connections. For deployments that need extra reliability, Redis Sentinel is enabled: it helps the system switch to a backup Redis server if the main one fails. The configured failover timeout is 30 seconds.

## Storing data efficiently

Cached data is encoded with MessagePack, a compact format for turning data into bytes and back again. Compression is turned off because tests found it added about 2 milliseconds to each operation. In this case, avoiding that extra delay is preferred.

## Watching cache health

Redis statistics are sent to Prometheus using `redis_exporter`, so the team can keep an eye on how the cache is doing. Useful measures include:

- **Connected clients:** how many applications or tools are connected.
- **Memory used:** how much memory Redis is using.
- **Cache hits and misses:** how often requested information was found in the cache versus not found.

A high number of hits often means the cache is saving repeat work. Misses are normal too: they happen when information has not been cached yet or has expired.

## Things to watch out for

- **Several requests may try to fill the same empty cache entry at once.** This can cause duplicate work during warm-up. Locks are used to help ensure only one request fills it at a time.
- **Very large values can use memory inefficiently.** Values larger than 1 MB may contribute to memory fragmentation. Splitting them into smaller pieces may help.
- **Redis messaging is not guaranteed delivery.** Its publish-and-subscribe feature is not suitable when every message must reliably arrive. The project uses Kafka for that kind of messaging instead.

## In short

Redis caching helps an app respond faster by keeping frequently needed information close at hand. Expiry times and updates help keep cached copies fresh, while connection reuse, backups, and monitoring help the cache run reliably. Because a cache is temporary, the app should still be able to recover important information from its main data source.

# API Endpoint Documentation

## User Endpoints

GET /api/v1/users
This endpoint returns a paginated list of all users in the system.
Authentication is required via Bearer token.
Query parameters: limit (default 20), offset (default 0), sort_by (name, created_at)
Returns: Array of user objects with id, name, email, created_at fields.

POST /api/v1/users
Creates a new user account in the system.
Requires admin role authentication.
Request body must include: name (string), email (string), role (string).
Optional fields: phone, department, manager_id.
Returns: Created user object with generated id.

GET /api/v1/users/{id}
Retrieves a single user by their unique identifier.
Authentication required. Users can only view their own profile unless admin.
Path parameter: id (UUID format required).
Returns: Full user object including preferences and metadata.

DELETE /api/v1/users/{id}
Permanently removes a user from the system.
Requires admin role. Cannot delete yourself.
Returns: 204 No Content on success.
Caution: This action cannot be undone.

## Redis Caching Implementation Notes

Cache invalidation strategy uses TTL-based expiry with write-through
on mutations. Key schema: `{entity_type}:{user_id}:{entity_id}`.

Connection pooling configured via redis-py with max_connections=50.
Sentinel support enabled for HA deployments. Failover timeout: 30s.

Serialization: msgpack for binary efficiency. Compression disabled
due to latency overhead (tested: ~2ms penalty per op).

Monitoring: Redis INFO stats exported to Prometheus via redis_exporter.
Key metrics: connected_clients, used_memory, keyspace_hits/misses.

Known issues:
- Race condition possible during cache warm-up (mitigated by locks)
- Large values (>1MB) cause fragmentation; consider chunking
- Pub/sub not suitable for reliable messaging; use Kafka instead

arguments.content:
# A Beginner’s Guide to Redis Caching

## What is caching?

Imagine you often need the same information, such as a user’s profile. Instead of looking it up in the main database every time, an application can keep a temporary copy somewhere it can reach quickly. That temporary copy is called a **cache**.

**Redis** is a tool that keeps data in memory, so applications can often retrieve cached information faster than fetching it from a database. This can make an app feel quicker and reduce repeated work for the database.

## How this project uses Redis

- **Keep cached data fresh:** Cached entries expire after a set amount of time (a TTL). When the app changes data, it also updates the cache. This helps prevent people from seeing old information for too long.
- **Organize entries:** Each cache key follows this pattern: `{entity_type}:{user_id}:{entity_id}`. A key is like a label that helps the app find the right cached item.
- **Reuse connections:** The app keeps a pool of Redis connections ready to use, with up to 50 connections. Reusing connections avoids repeatedly setting them up.
- **Stay available:** Redis Sentinel helps monitor Redis servers and supports switching to another server if the current one fails. The configured failover timeout is 30 seconds.
- **Store data efficiently:** Cached data is encoded with MessagePack, a compact format for turning data into bytes and back again. Compression is turned off because testing showed it adds about 2 milliseconds to each operation.
- **Watch how it is doing:** Redis statistics are sent to Prometheus using `redis_exporter`. The team watches how many clients are connected, how much memory Redis uses, and how often requests find or miss cached data.

## Things to keep in mind

- When the cache is first filled, two requests might try to load the same data at once. Locks help prevent that race.
- Very large cached values (over 1 MB) can use memory inefficiently. Splitting them into smaller pieces may help.
- Redis publish-and-subscribe messages are not guaranteed to be delivered reliably. For important messages that must not be lost, use Kafka instead.

In short, Redis caching keeps frequently needed data close at hand. Used carefully, it can make an application faster while reducing repeated database work. The cache is a temporary helper, so the application should still be able to get the real data from its main source when needed.

Authentication required. Users can only view their own profile unless admin.
Path parameter: id (UUID format required).

Permanently removes a user from the system.
Requires admin role. Cannot delete yourself.
Returns: 204 No Content on success.
Caution: This action cannot be undone.

## Redis Caching Implementation Notes

Cache invalidation strategy uses TTL-based expiry with write-through
on mutations. Key schema: `{entity_type}:{user_id}:{entity_id}`.

Connection pooling configured via redis-py with max_connections=50.
Sentinel support enabled for HA deployments. Failover timeout: 30s.

Serialization: msgpack for binary efficiency. Compression disabled
due to latency overhead (tested: ~2ms penalty per op).

Monitoring: Redis INFO stats exported to Prometheus via redis_exporter.
Key metrics: connected_clients, used_memory, keyspace_hits/misses.

Known issues:
- Race condition possible during cache warm-up (mitigated by locks)
- Large values (>1MB) cause fragmentation; consider chunking
- Pub/sub not suitable for reliable messaging; use Kafka instead

arguments.content:
## Redis Caching: A Beginner-Friendly Guide

### What is caching?

Imagine you often need to look up the same information. Instead of going back to a large filing cabinet every time, you keep a handy copy nearby. A cache works in a similar way: it stores copies of information that an application may need again soon, so the application can retrieve them quickly.

Redis is a tool commonly used to hold this fast, temporary data. Caching can make an app feel quicker and reduce repeated work for the systems that store the original information.

### How this setup works

- **Cached information expires automatically.** Each saved item has a time limit (called a TTL). When the time is up, Redis removes it, helping prevent old copies from sticking around forever.
- **Changes update the cache.** When the app changes information, it also updates the cached copy. This helps people see recent data rather than an outdated version.
- **Keys help find the right item.** Each cached item gets a label built from its type, the user, and the item's ID—for example, `profile:42:7`. This makes it easier to keep different users' items separate and look up a specific one.
- **Connections are reused.** The app keeps a pool of up to 50 Redis connections ready to use, rather than repeatedly opening new ones. This can save time when many requests arrive.
- **There is a backup plan for availability.** Redis Sentinel helps the system notice if a Redis server has a problem and switch to another one. The configured failover timeout is 30 seconds.
- **Data is stored in a compact format.** The app uses MessagePack, a format that turns data into a compact form Redis can store and return. Compression is turned off because tests showed it added about 2 milliseconds to each operation.

### Keeping an eye on the cache

Monitoring tools collect information about Redis and send it to Prometheus, where the team can track how it is doing. Useful measurements include how many clients are connected, how much memory Redis is using, and how often requests find (or miss) an item in the cache.

### Things to watch out for

- **Starting the cache can cause a rush of requests.** If many requests try to fill the cache at once, they can overlap. Locks help make sure only one process fills a particular item at a time.
- **Very large items can use memory inefficiently.** Values larger than 1 MB may cause memory fragmentation. Splitting them into smaller pieces may help.
- **Redis messaging is not guaranteed delivery.** Its publish-and-subscribe feature is useful for quick notifications, but messages can be missed. For important messages that must be delivered reliably, use Kafka instead.

### In short

Redis caching keeps frequently needed information close at hand so an application can respond faster and avoid repeating work. Expiration and updates help keep cached copies fresh, while monitoring and backup arrangements help the team operate the cache reliably.
